Resolving this matters because an Irish origin opens a distinct body of emigration and origin records — Irish church registers, civil registration, and Griffith's Valuation — that could corroborate his parentage, the central research objective.

The 1850 U.S. Census, recorded by an enumerator who visited the Thomas Flynn household when Patrick was approximately 5 years old, lists his birthplace as Ireland. The 1860 U.S. Census, a separate enumeration ten years later by a different enumerator, again lists Patrick as born in Ireland, now age 15 and still in the Thomas Flynn household. Both censuses were recorded from information supplied by whoever answered the enumerator — most likely Thomas Flynn or his wife. Patrick's 1908 death certificate states his birthplace as Pennsylvania. The informant for that fact was James Brown, Patrick's son-in-law, who signed the certificate.

The census evidence is more reliable on three grounds. The household informants who answered the census enumerators in 1850 and 1860 had direct personal knowledge of Patrick's origins: they either witnessed the birth or emigrated from Ireland with him as a young child. The 1850 census was taken only about five years after Patrick's birth — the family's memory of being Irish-born would have been fresh and present. James Brown could not have had any firsthand knowledge of a birth that occurred decades before he joined the family as a son-in-law. The death certificate was created 63 years after the birth, by a non-witness reporting what he thought he knew. Two contemporaneous recordings by independent enumerators, both giving Ireland, clearly outweigh a single late report by a non-witness. The GPS preponderance under the combination rationale (uncorroborated single item plus more error-prone information) favors Ireland, with a_002 as the preferred assertion.

The 'Pennsylvania' entry on the death certificate is explained by the immigration origin confusion and memory degradation patterns documented in historical research. James Brown knew Patrick exclusively as a Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania resident — every record from 1850 to 1908 places Patrick in Pennsylvania. Brown had no reason to know, and likely did not know, that Patrick was born in Ireland and arrived in Pennsylvania as a young child. When asked for Patrick's birthplace, Brown almost certainly reported the only place he associated with his father-in-law. This is a well-documented pattern for Irish immigrants who arrived as young children: their American-raised relatives and in-laws knew them only as Americans and reported their longtime state of residence as birthplace. A son-in-law reporting a birth he did not witness, more than six decades after the event, about a man he knew only in his mature Pennsylvania life, is precisely the informant most susceptible to this error.

fields.independence_analysis: The three competing assertions fall into two groups by informant. The 1850 and 1860 census birthplace claims (a_002, a_009) are recorded in independent source records — different enumerators, different years, different census schedules — but the underlying knowledge almost certainly traces to the same informants: Thomas Flynn or his wife, reporting their child's birthplace on two separate census occasions ten years apart. Per GPS Standard 46, these two assertions must be treated as a partially dependent unit, counted as no more than one strong report. The death certificate birthplace claim (a_012) originates from a wholly different informant — James Brown, Patrick's son-in-law — and is fully independent of the census records. The conflict therefore reduces to two sides: one partially dependent census unit (Ireland) versus one independent death certificate entry (Pennsylvania).
fields.weighing_analysis: Three factors decisively favor the Ireland claims. First, informant proximity: the census household informants — almost certainly Thomas Flynn and/or his wife — are the people with the most direct possible knowledge of Patrick's birthplace, since parents are as close to eyewitness knowledge of a child's origins as exists. James Brown, the death certificate informant, was Patrick's son-in-law: he entered the family as an adult and cannot have had any firsthand knowledge of a birth predating his relationship with the family by decades. Second, time lag: the 1850 census was recorded roughly five years after Patrick's estimated 1845 birth, and the 1860 census roughly fifteen years later — both within living memory of the likely informants. The death certificate was created in 1908, sixty-three years after the birth. Memory and transmitted family lore degrade markedly over such intervals. Third, corroboration: both original census records agree on Ireland, representing two independent recording occasions by different enumerators. The Pennsylvania claim stands alone with a secondary informant. The applicable defensible rationale is a combination of Standard 48 rationales 1 and 2: the death certificate birthplace entry is uncorroborated and comes from a more error-prone informant — secondary, with no firsthand knowledge — while two independent recording occasions by proximate informants corroborate Ireland.

Patrick Flynn's birthplace is disputed between Ireland (1850 and 1860 censuses, a_002 and a_009) and Pennsylvania (1908 death certificate, a_012). The correct birthplace matters for tracing Patrick's immigrant origins and for assessing the quality of the parentage evidence; it also needs formal resolution because the proof summary (ps_001) lists this conflict as resolved while the conflict record itself remained open.

Two original census records name Ireland. The 1850 schedule (a_002) was recorded by a census enumerator who visited the Thomas Flynn household approximately five years after Patrick's estimated 1845 birth; the informant was almost certainly Thomas Flynn or his wife — the people with the most direct possible knowledge of where their child was born. The 1860 schedule (a_009) records the same fact fifteen years after the birth, again from the Thomas Flynn household. Both are original government records taken from household members with close personal knowledge of the birth. The 1908 death certificate (a_012) states Pennsylvania. Its informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. Brown married into the family as an adult and had no firsthand knowledge of a birth that occurred roughly sixty-three years before he completed the certificate. He was a secondary informant for all biographical facts about Patrick's origins.

The census records are strongly preferred. The informants closest in relationship and time to Patrick's birth — his likely parents, speaking in 1850 and again in 1860 — consistently named Ireland. No motive for misstatement is apparent; Ireland was the same answer on two separate recording occasions to two different enumerators. James Brown, by contrast, was grieving, reporting under the administrative pressure of a death certificate, and could not have witnessed the birth.

The Pennsylvania entry is best explained by immigration origin confusion, a well-documented pattern in American death certificates for Irish-born immigrants of the mid-19th century. Brown would have known Patrick grew up in Pennsylvania and identified as part of the Irish immigrant community, but the precise distinction between 'born in Ireland, immigrated as a young child' and 'born in Pennsylvania of Irish descent' was not within his direct knowledge. A son-in-law reporting a birth he did not witness, sixty-three years after the fact, for a man who emigrated from Ireland as a very young child and spent his entire documented adult life in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — where Pennsylvania was the family's entire lived experience — is a classic context for conflating birthplace with place of upbringing. Pennsylvania was the obvious, locally familiar answer to 'where was he from,' even if it collapsed birth country with country of residence. Ireland is accepted as Patrick's birthplace; a_002 is the preferred assertion.

fields.resolution_rationale:
Patrick Flynn's birthplace is disputed between Ireland (1850 and 1860 censuses, a_002 and a_009) and Pennsylvania (1908 death certificate, a_012). The correct birthplace matters for tracing Patrick's immigrant origins and for assessing the quality of the parentage evidence; it also needs formal resolution because the proof summary (ps_001) lists this conflict as resolved while the conflict record itself remained open.

Two original census records name Ireland. The 1850 schedule (a_002) was recorded by a census enumerator who visited the Thomas Flynn household approximately five years after Patrick's estimated 1845 birth; the informant was almost certainly Thomas Flynn or his wife — the people with the most direct possible knowledge of where their child was born. The 1860 schedule (a_009) records the same fact fifteen years after the birth, again from the Thomas Flynn household. Both are original government records taken from household members with close personal knowledge of the birth. The 1908 death certificate (a_012) states Pennsylvania. Its informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. Brown married into the family as an adult and had no firsthand knowledge of a birth that occurred roughly sixty-three years before he completed the certificate. He was a secondary informant for all biographical facts about Patrick's origins.

The census records are strongly preferred. The informants closest in relationship and time to Patrick's birth — his likely parents, speaking in 1850 and again in 1860 — consistently named Ireland. No motive for misstatement is apparent; Ireland was the same answer on two separate recording occasions to two different enumerators. James Brown, by contrast, was grieving, reporting under the administrative pressure of a death certificate, and could not have witnessed the birth.

The Pennsylvania entry is best explained by immigration origin confusion, a well-documented pattern in American death certificates for Irish-born immigrants of the mid-19th century. Brown would have known Patrick grew up in Pennsylvania and identified as part of the Irish immigrant community, but the precise distinction between 'born in Ireland, immigrated as a young child' and 'born in Pennsylvania of Irish descent' was not within his direct knowledge. A son-in-law reporting a birth he did not witness, sixty-three years after the fact, for a man who emigrated from Ireland as a very young child and spent his entire documented adult life in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — where Pennsylvania was the family's entire lived experience — is a classic context for conflating birthplace with place of upbringing. Pennsylvania was the obvious, locally familiar answer to 'where was he from,' even if it collapsed birth country with country of residence. Ireland is accepted as Patrick's birthplace; a_002 is the preferred assertion.
